chapterTitle: Milk, Fields and Fire — God's Farm, God's Building, God's Temple
themeTitle: “The Fire Will Not Ask How Big It Was — Only What It Was Made Of”

scripture.text: Brothers, I couldn’t speak to you as to spiritual, but as to fleshly, as to babies in Christ.
scripture.understanding: Paul turns the last verse of chapter 2 on its head. They claimed to be πνευματικοί, spiritual people — and he says he could not speak to them that way. Instead they were σάρκινοι, made of flesh, and νήπιοι, infants. The word means literally “not speaking,” a child too young to talk. Corinth was proud of its eloquence, and Paul tells them that spiritually they had not learned to talk yet. Notice, though: “babies in Christ.” They are in Christ. The rebuke is to real believers who never grew up.

scripture.text: I fed you with milk, not with meat; for you weren’t yet ready. Indeed, not even now are you ready,
scripture.understanding: Γάλα, milk, and βρῶμα, solid food. When Paul first came, milk was right; you do not feed steak to a newborn. The problem is the next sentence: “Indeed, not even now are you ready.” Years have passed. They have gifts, teachers, knowledge, and tongues. And they still need a bottle. Spiritual age is not measured by how long you have been a Christian or how much you know. It is measured by what you can digest.

scripture.text: for you are still fleshly. For insofar as there is jealousy, strife, and factions among you, aren’t you fleshly, and don’t you walk in the ways of men?
scripture.understanding: The proof of immaturity is not lack of knowledge but the presence of ζῆλος, jealousy, and ἔρις, strife. And here the word changes to σαρκικοί, fleshly in character — not just made of flesh but governed by it. Then a cutting question: “don’t you walk in the ways of men?” The Greek says “walk according to man” — you are living like ordinary unconverted people. They thought their gifts proved they were spiritual. Paul says their quarrels proved they were not.

scripture.text: For when one says, “I follow Paul,” and another, “I follow Apollos,” aren’t you fleshly?
scripture.understanding: Paul names the slogans again from 1:12 — “I follow Paul,” “I follow Apollos” — and attaches them to the diagnosis. Party spirit is not a sign of spiritual seriousness. It is a symptom of the flesh. When you need a human leader to define your identity, you are acting like a child who needs to say whose gang he belongs to.

scripture.text: Who then is Apollos, and who is Paul, but servants through whom you believed; and each as the Lord gave to him?
scripture.understanding: “Who then is Apollos, and who is Paul?” Notice he says “who” in some manuscripts and “what” in others — and the point is the same either way: they are διάκονοι, servants. The word originally meant a table waiter. That is all the great preachers are: waiters bringing the food. And each did only what “the Lord gave to him.” Nobody fights over which waiter brought the meal. You thank the one who cooked it.

scripture.text: I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase.
scripture.understanding: Three verbs and three tenses. Paul φυτεύω, planted — a single past act, the founding of the church. Apollos ποτίζω, watered — also completed. But God αὐξάνω — and here the tense changes to the imperfect: God was giving the growth, continuously, all along. The men did their moments. God was doing the work the whole time.

scripture.text: So then neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase.
scripture.understanding: The conclusion is humbling for everyone in ministry: neither the planter nor the waterer “is anything.” Not that their work is useless — Paul works harder than anyone — but that, compared to the One who makes things grow, they are not the point. No farmer has ever made a seed sprout. He can plant and water. Life comes from somewhere else.

scripture.text: Now he who plants and he who waters are the same, but each will receive his own reward according to his own labor.
scripture.understanding: The planter and the waterer “are the same” — literally “are one.” They are not rivals but one team with one purpose. Yet each will receive his own μισθός, wages, “according to his own κόπος,” labour. Note what is rewarded: not results but toil. God pays for faithful labour, not for visible success. The man who planted and saw nothing grow will be paid for his planting.

scripture.text: For we are God’s fellow workers. You are God’s farming, God’s building.
scripture.understanding: Three times “God's” in one verse, each placed first in the Greek for emphasis: God's fellow workers, God's farm, God's building. Συνεργός — co-workers, from which we get synergy. The great honour of ministry is not that you are important, but that you get to work alongside God in His field. Γεώργιον is a cultivated field; οἰκοδομή is a building under construction. The image now switches from agriculture to architecture.

scripture.text: According to the grace of God which was given to me, as a wise master builder I laid a foundation, and another builds on it. But let each man be careful how he builds on it.
scripture.understanding: Ἀρχιτέκτων — chief builder, master craftsman, the root of our word architect. Paul calls himself “wise” — after two chapters of attacking wisdom — but he immediately grounds it in “the grace of God which was given to me.” He laid the θεμέλιος, the foundation, and others ἐποικοδομέω, build on top of it. Then the warning that governs the next five verses: “let each man be careful how he builds on it.” Not whether, but how.

scripture.text: For no one can lay any other foundation than that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ.
scripture.understanding: There is only one foundation, and it has already been laid: Jesus Christ. No one can lay another one. Every true church, every true ministry, every true Christian life stands on the same rock. The question is never whether you have the right foundation if you are in Christ. The question is what you are putting on top of it.

scripture.text: But if anyone builds on the foundation with gold, silver, costly stones, wood, hay, or stubble;
scripture.understanding: Two sets of three materials. Gold, silver, costly stones — precious, durable, fireproof. Wood, hay, stubble — cheap, quick, and combustible. The list descends in value and rises in flammability. You could build a hut of straw in an afternoon; a temple of marble takes years. The temptation in ministry and in life is always to build fast and cheap and impressive-looking. Paul says the materials will be tested.

scripture.text: each man’s work will be revealed. For the Day will declare it, because it is revealed in fire; and the fire itself will test what sort of work each man’s work is.
scripture.understanding: “The Day” — the Day of the Lord, the day of judgment — will δηλόω, make it plain. It is revealed in πῦρ, fire, and the fire δοκιμάζω — tests, assays, the word used for testing metal in a furnace. Notice what is tested: “what sort” of work it is — its quality, not its size. Corinth was impressed by quantity, noise and display. The fire will not ask how big it was, only what it was made of.

scripture.text: If any man’s work remains which he built on it, he will receive a reward.
scripture.understanding: If the work μένω — remains, survives the fire — the builder receives a reward. Paul does not define the reward here, and it is wise not to speculate beyond him. What is certain is that faithful work done on Christ will survive the Day of judgment, and that God will acknowledge it.

scripture.text: If any man’s work is burned, he will suffer loss, but he himself will be saved, but as through fire.
scripture.understanding: Κατακαίω — burned down completely. If the work is consumed, the builder ζημιόω, suffers loss — he forfeits the reward. “But he himself will be saved, but as through fire.” The picture is of a man escaping a burning house with nothing but his life. This verse is about believers — people built on Christ — whose works are tested, not about unbelievers, and it is about works being tested, not souls being purged. It offers no support for the later doctrine of purgatory. It does offer a sobering possibility: a saved life with nothing to show for it.

scripture.text: Don’t you know that you are a temple of God, and that God’s Spirit lives in you?
scripture.understanding: The image tightens one more time: from field, to building, to ναός — not the whole temple complex but the inner sanctuary, the holy place where God's presence dwelt. And the “you” is plural: you, together, are a temple of God. The church gathered in Corinth was the place where God lived. “Don’t you know?” — Paul asks this ten times in this letter. They knew so much, and they had forgotten the most basic things.

scripture.text: If anyone destroys God’s temple, God will destroy him; for God’s temple is holy, which you are.
scripture.understanding: The most severe warning in the chapter, and it is a play on one verb: “If anyone φθείρω — ruins, corrupts, destroys — God’s temple, God will φθείρω him.” The context is division. The people tearing the Corinthian church apart with factions were not merely being unpleasant; they were vandalising God's house, and God takes that personally. “God’s temple is holy, which you are.” A church is not a club you can break. It is a sanctuary you can desecrate.

scripture.text: Let no one deceive himself. If anyone thinks that he is wise among you in this world, let him become a fool, that he may become wise.
scripture.understanding: “Let no one deceive himself.” Ἐξαπατάω — thoroughly deceive, the word Paul uses of the serpent deceiving Eve (2 Corinthians 11:3). Self-deception is the subtlest kind. Anyone who thinks he is wise by the standards of this age must become a μωρός — a fool in the world's eyes — in order to become truly wise. The way up is down. You cannot add the cross to your existing wisdom. You have to let it overturn it.

scripture.text: For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. For it is written, “He has taken the wise in their craftiness.”
scripture.understanding: Paul quotes Job 5:13, from the speech of Eliphaz — one of Job's friends whose overall counsel God later rebukes. But Paul cites this particular statement as Scripture, and it is true: God δράσσομαι, catches, the clever in their πανουργία, their craftiness, their trickery. The schemes that seem smartest are the very nets in which God catches the schemers.

scripture.text: And again, “The Lord knows the reasoning of the wise, that it is worthless.”
scripture.understanding: A second quotation, from Psalm 94:11. The Lord knows the διαλογισμοί — the reasonings, the internal calculations — of the wise, and that they are μάταιοι: empty, futile, vain. The Hebrew of the psalm says the thoughts of man; Paul applies it to the wise, which is exactly the category Corinth admired.

scripture.text: Therefore let no one boast in men. For all things are yours,
scripture.understanding: The conclusion of the first major section of the letter: “let no one boast in men.” And then the astonishing reason: “For all things are yours.” They were trying to belong to Paul or Apollos. Paul reverses it. You do not belong to them. They belong to you.

scripture.text: whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas, or the world, or life, or death, or things present, or things to come. All are yours,
scripture.understanding: The list explodes outward. Paul, Apollos, Cephas — the leaders they were fighting over. Then the world, life, death, things present, things to come — everything in existence and everything in time. All of it is yours. Death is yours: it serves you now, the door into Christ's presence. The future is yours. Why would anyone shrink themselves into a faction when the whole universe has been put at their service?

scripture.text: and you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s.
scripture.understanding: And then the order of ownership: you are Christ's, and Christ is God's. Everything belongs to you because you belong to Christ, and Christ belongs to the Father. You are not the top of the chain; you are owned. But you are owned by the One who owns everything. That is why no human loyalty can compete. You already have the best master there is.

visualMeditations.title: A Baby With a Beard
visualMeditations.image: Picture a grown man — broad shoulders, a beard, a booming voice, an expensive coat — sitting in a high chair and crying for his bottle. He can recite poetry, debate philosophy and quote whole chapters of Scripture. But put two other men in the room who get more attention than he does and he throws his food on the floor. That is what Paul sees when he looks at Corinth. Gifted. Knowledgeable. Articulate. And spiritually still in nappies, fighting over whose turn it is.
visualMeditations.meaning: Paul's diagnosis of spiritual immaturity is not what most people expect. He does not say the Corinthians lacked knowledge; they had plenty. He does not say they lacked gifts; they lacked none (1:7). He says the evidence of their infancy was jealousy and strife. Maturity is not measured by what you know, how long you have been saved, or how spectacular your gifts are. It is measured by how you treat people who are honoured more than you. A Christian who cannot rejoice when someone else is praised is still drinking milk, no matter how much he can quote.

visualMeditations.title: The Farmer Who Cannot Make Anything Grow
visualMeditations.image: Watch two farmers in the same field. The first one ploughs and plants in early spring — back bent, hands blistered, seed bag on his hip. Weeks later the second one comes with buckets from the stream and waters every row through the dry months. Then one morning both of them stand at the edge of the field and watch green shoots breaking the soil. Neither of them made it happen. Neither of them could have. They could put the seed in the ground and water it, but the life inside the seed, the miracle of germination, the push of a green stem through soil — that came from God. And it was happening the whole time they were working.
visualMeditations.meaning: The tense of the verbs in verse 6 is the sermon. Paul planted (once). Apollos watered (once). God was giving the growth (continuously). The human contributions were moments; the divine work was constant. That changes how you see every ministry, including your own. You are responsible for planting and watering — faithfully, carefully, without cutting corners. You are not responsible for the growth, and you cannot produce it. If you take credit for it, you are stealing from God. If you despair because you cannot see it yet, you are forgetting who is working underground. And notice verse 8: you are paid for your labour, not your harvest.

visualMeditations.title: The City That Had Burned
visualMeditations.image: The Corinthians knew what fire did to a city. In 146 BC the Roman general Mummius had captured old Corinth, and the city was sacked and burned. Picture it: wooden roofs collapsing, thatched sheds turning to ash in seconds, the smoke visible for miles across the gulf. When the flames died down, the wood, hay and straw were gone. What remained standing were the stone columns — some of the columns of the old Temple of Apollo still stand in Corinth today — and the metal that had melted and pooled in the rubble. Now picture the Day of the Lord as a fire like that, passing over every life built on Christ. Some lives come through it like stone. Others vanish like a straw roof, and the builder runs out of the burning house with nothing but the clothes he is wearing.
visualMeditations.meaning: This is not a picture of unbelievers being judged; they are not on the foundation at all. It is a picture of believers whose works are being tested. Everyone in view is building on Christ. The question is the material. Gold, silver and costly stones are slow, expensive and durable — work done with pure motives, in obedience, with love, according to the truth. Wood, hay and stubble are quick, cheap and impressive for a while — work done for applause, for numbers, in the flesh, with shortcuts. The fire tests “what sort” of work it is, not how big it is. And verse 15 is one of the most sobering sentences Paul ever wrote: it is possible to be saved and yet arrive with nothing.

visualMeditations.title: The Sanctuary in the Courtyard
visualMeditations.image: In Jerusalem, at the centre of the great temple complex with its courts and porches and crowds, there was an inner sanctuary — the ναός — where the presence of God dwelt. Only priests entered the Holy Place, and only the high priest entered the Holy of Holies, once a year, with blood. Now picture a small group of believers gathered in a courtyard in Corinth on a Sunday evening: slaves, dockworkers, a few wealthier families, all quarrelling about which preacher was best. Paul looks at that room and says: this is the ναός. Here is where God lives now.
visualMeditations.meaning: The “you” in verses 16 and 17 is plural. Paul is not yet talking about the individual body (that comes in 6:19). He is talking about the gathered church as the sanctuary of God's presence. And the warning is terrifying precisely because of that: whoever destroys — corrupts, ruins — God's temple, God will destroy him. The context is division. The people splitting Corinth into parties thought they were having a debate about preachers. Paul says they were vandalising the Holy of Holies. Treat the church — the actual, flawed, frustrating people you worship with — as the dwelling of God, because it is.

structure.label: Still Infants (v. 1-4)
structure.body: Paul could not speak to them as spiritual people because they were still fleshly — babies who need milk — and the proof was their jealousy, strife and factions over human leaders.

structure.label: Servants in God's Field (v. 5-9)
structure.body: Paul and Apollos are only servants; one planted, one watered, but God gave the growth — so the workers are one, each rewarded for his labour, all of them God's fellow workers in God's field.

structure.label: Builders on One Foundation (v. 10-15)
structure.body: Paul laid the only foundation, Jesus Christ; everyone else must take care how they build on it, because the Day will test each one's work by fire — some will be rewarded, others will suffer loss though they themselves are saved.

structure.label: The Temple of God (v. 16-17)
structure.body: The church together is God's sanctuary where His Spirit lives; whoever destroys it will be destroyed by God.

structure.label: All Things Are Yours (v. 18-23)
structure.body: Abandon worldly wisdom; stop boasting in men; everything — leaders, the world, life, death, present and future — belongs to you, because you belong to Christ, and Christ belongs to God.

sections.heading: The Measure of Maturity: Not What You Know but How You Treat Rivals
paragraphs: Chapter 3 opens with one of the most deflating sentences ever written to a church. The Corinthians believed they were πνευματικοί, spiritual people — the very word Paul had just used in 2:15. They had tongues, prophecy, knowledge, and eloquent teachers. And Paul says, in effect: I could not talk to you that way. You were σάρκινοι — made of flesh — and νήπιοι, babies. Worse: “Indeed, not even now are you ready.” This is not a description of new converts. Paul had spent eighteen months with them, Apollos had taught them since, and several years had passed. They had been Christians long enough to be eating meat, and they were still on milk.

What is the evidence? Not lack of information — they were proud of their knowledge. Not lack of experience — they had more spiritual gifts than any church Paul wrote to. The evidence is verse 3: “insofar as there is jealousy, strife, and factions among you, aren’t you fleshly, and don’t you walk in the ways of men?” Paul's word shifts from σάρκινος (made of flesh) in verse 1 to σαρκικός (characterised by the flesh) in verse 3, and the point sharpens: being made of flesh is not a sin, but being governed by it is. Their quarrels about preachers were not a sign of theological seriousness. They were the behaviour of ordinary unconverted people. “Walk according to man,” the Greek says — you are living as if the cross had never happened.

This reframes spiritual maturity entirely. In Corinth, and in many churches today, maturity is measured by gifts, knowledge, years of service or public visibility. Paul measures it by the presence or absence of jealousy and strife. The writer of Hebrews makes a similar diagnosis — “You have come to need milk, and not solid food” (Hebrews 5:12) — and defines maturity as having “senses exercised to discern good and evil” (5:14). Maturity is not a bigger head. It is a trained conscience and a heart that can rejoice when someone else is honoured. If you want to know how mature you are, do not ask how much you know. Ask how you respond when the person you consider your rival is praised in front of you.

sections.heading: Wood, Hay and Stubble: The Coming Fire and What It Will Test
paragraphs: Verses 10 to 15 are among the most important verses in the New Testament about the judgment of believers, and they are frequently misunderstood in two opposite directions. First, be clear about who is in view. Everyone in this passage is building on the foundation, “which is Jesus Christ” (v. 11). This is not about the final judgment of unbelievers. It is about the evaluation of the work of believers — and in the immediate context, especially the work of those who teach and lead the church, since Paul is talking about himself, Apollos and those who build after them. Paul will say the same thing in his second letter to this church: “For we must all be revealed before the judgment seat of Christ; that each one may receive the things in the body, according to what he has done, whether good or bad” (2 Corinthians 5:10).

Second, notice what is tested. Not the person's salvation — that rests on the foundation, which cannot be shaken. What is tested is “what sort of work each man’s work is” (v. 13). The quality, not the quantity. The six materials of verse 12 are a deliberate contrast: gold, silver and costly stones are precious and fireproof; wood, hay and stubble are cheap and burn instantly. You can build a straw hut in an afternoon and it will look like a building. A stone temple takes years. Paul does not define the materials precisely, and it is better not to over-allegorise them. But the rest of the letter shows what he has in mind: work built with the wisdom of the cross versus the wisdom of the world; work done in love versus work done for self (chapter 13); teaching that is true versus teaching that flatters. The Day will reveal it, because God “will both bring to light the hidden things of darkness, and reveal the counsels of the hearts” (4:5). Motives are part of the material.

Third, be honest about verse 15, because it has been bent out of shape. Some later traditions used it to support the doctrine of purgatory — a process of purifying souls after death. But the fire here tests works, not people; it happens on “the Day,” not over a period after death; and the person is “saved” already, with the fire describing the manner of his escape, not a process that saves him. The image is of a man running out of a burning house with his life and nothing else. That should sober every believer. It is possible to be truly saved and yet to stand before Christ having built a life that does not survive the fire — a life of busy, visible, impressive straw. The question is not whether you are building. Everyone is. The question is what you are building with.

sections.heading: You Do Not Belong to Them — They Belong to You
paragraphs: Verses 16 and 17 lift the stakes of division higher than anyone in Corinth had imagined. The church is not just a field or a building; it is the ναός, the inner sanctuary, the place where God's presence lives. In the Old Testament, the presence of God dwelt in the tabernacle and then in the temple in Jerusalem. Now, Paul says, it dwells in the gathered people of God. That is why the warning of verse 17 is so severe. Φθείρω means to ruin, corrupt or destroy, and Paul uses it twice in the same sentence: whoever ruins God's temple, God will ruin. The people who were splitting the church into rival factions were not merely being disagreeable. They were defacing God's house, and God takes the vandalism of His sanctuary personally. Notice that Paul does not say this about pagans attacking the church from outside. He says it about members tearing it apart from within.

Then Paul brings the whole section, chapters 1 to 3, to a close. “Let no one deceive himself” (v. 18). The Corinthians believed that attaching themselves to the right teacher made them wise. Paul tells them that real wisdom begins by becoming a fool in the world's eyes — by accepting the message of the cross that the world laughs at. He quotes two Old Testament texts. Job 5:13 says God catches the wise in their own craftiness; Psalm 94:11 says the Lord knows the reasonings of the wise are futile. (It is worth noting honestly that the first comes from Eliphaz, one of Job's friends whose overall counsel God rebukes in Job 42:7. Paul is not endorsing everything Eliphaz said; he is citing a statement that is true and consistent with the rest of Scripture.)

And then the breathtaking conclusion: “Therefore let no one boast in men. For all things are yours, whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas, or the world, or life, or death, or things present, or things to come. All are yours, and you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s” (vv. 21–23). The Corinthians had their ownership upside down. They thought they belonged to their leaders — “I am of Paul.” Paul says the leaders belong to them; they are gifts God gave for the church's good. Everything belongs to them: the world, life, even death, which now serves the believer as the door into Christ's presence. Why would anyone shrink themselves down to the size of a party when the whole universe has been placed at their service? And yet the chain does not end with “you.” You are Christ's, and Christ is God's. You are free from every human master because you have been bought by the only Master who matters.

ntConnection.heading: New Testament Connection
paragraphs: Paul's foundation of verse 11 has its root in the words of Jesus Himself. At the end of the Sermon on the Mount Jesus told the story of two builders: “Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine, and does them, I will liken him to a wise man, who built his house on a rock. The rain came down, the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat on that house; and it didn’t fall, for it was founded on the rock” (Matthew 7:24–25). Jesus' story tests the foundation; Paul's passage tests the building on top of it. Together they cover both questions: are you on the rock, and what are you building there? And Peter, preaching before the very council that condemned Jesus, called Him “the stone which was regarded as worthless by you, the builders, which has become the head of the corner” (Acts 4:11). The rejected stone is the only foundation.

The temple image of verses 16 and 17 grows across the New Testament. Jesus Himself said, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up,” and John explains, “But he spoke of the temple of his body” (John 2:19, 21). The presence of God that dwelt in the tabernacle and the Jerusalem temple came to live in the body of Jesus. Then, through the Spirit, that dwelling extends to His people. Paul tells the Ephesians they are “built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the chief cornerstone; in whom the whole building, fitted together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord; in whom you also are built together for a habitation of God in the Spirit” (Ephesians 2:20–22). Peter says the same: “You also, as living stones, are built up as a spiritual house, to be a holy priesthood” (1 Peter 2:5). And at the end of the story the image reaches its fulfilment: “I saw no temple in it, for the Lord God, the Almighty, and the Lamb, are its temple” (Revelation 21:22).

And the judgment of believers' works in verses 13 to 15 is repeated in Romans, written from Corinth a few years later: “But you, why do you judge your brother? Or you again, why do you despise your brother? For we will all stand before the judgment seat of Christ… So then each one of us will give account of himself to God” (Romans 14:10, 12). Notice how Paul uses this truth in both letters: not to frighten believers about their salvation but to stop them judging and despising each other. If each of us will give account of our own building, we have no business tearing down someone else's. The coming fire is the best argument against present factions.

lexicon.insight: Strong's: “not speaking, i.e. an infant (minor); figuratively, a simple-minded person, an immature Christian.” The word is built from a negative prefix and a root meaning to speak — literally a child too young to talk. The irony would not have been lost on Corinth, a church that prided itself on eloquence and on speaking in tongues. Spiritually, Paul says, you have not learned to speak yet. Paul uses the same word positively in 14:20 — “in malice be babies, but in thoughts be mature.” There is a right way to be a child: innocent of evil. Corinth had chosen the wrong way: immature in understanding and sophisticated in quarrelling.

Strong's defines σαρκικός as “pertaining to flesh, i.e. (by extension) bodily, temporal, or (by implication) animal, unregenerate,” and σάρκινος as “similar to flesh.” The difference matters. In verse 1, Paul says they were σάρκινοι — made of flesh, as every newborn is; that is simply their condition as infants. In verse 3 he says they are still σαρκικοί — characterised and governed by the flesh, which is a moral charge. A baby is not to blame for being a baby. A grown man who still behaves like one is. The progression from verse 1 to verse 3 is the progression from a season of immaturity, which is normal, to a refusal to grow, which is not.

Strong's: “a co-laborer, i.e. coadjutor.” This is the word from which English gets synergy — working together. Paul uses it of his ministry partners repeatedly — Priscilla and Aquila are his συνεργοί (Romans 16:3), Timothy is his συνεργός (Romans 16:21). Here he uses it of himself and Apollos in relation to God: “we are God’s fellow workers.” The honour of ministry is not that God needs you but that He invites you to work alongside Him in His field. A servant who understands that will never compete with another servant. You do not fight with the other workers in your master's field. You work beside them.

Strong's: “to test (literally or figuratively); by implication, to approve.” In ordinary Greek this was the word for assaying metal — testing gold and silver in a furnace to see whether they were genuine. The same family gives us δόκιμος, approved, the word Paul uses in 2 Timothy 2:15 for a worker “approved by God.” Notice that the purpose of testing is approval, not destruction. Gold put through the fire comes out purer and proven. The fire of verse 13 is not God's way of hunting for faults; it is His way of revealing what was real. The only things it destroys are things that were never going to last anyway.

Strong's: “a fane, shrine, temple.” The New Testament has two main words for temple. Ἱερόν refers to the whole temple complex with its courts and porches — the place where Jesus overturned tables. Ναός refers to the sanctuary itself, the dwelling of God, the Holy Place and the Holy of Holies. Paul uses ναός here, and again in 6:19 and 2 Corinthians 6:16. The church is not just a religious complex where people gather. It is the inner sanctuary where God dwells. That is why division is not a minor problem in Paul's eyes. To tear the church apart is to tear down the walls of the Holy of Holies.

holySpiritRevelation.intro: The Spirit is dealing with three things in this chapter: the immaturity you have mistaken for spirituality, the materials you are actually building your life with, and the people in your church you have stopped treating as God's dwelling place.

items.title: Still on Milk
items.body: You may know a great deal of Scripture. You may have been a Christian for years. You may serve, pray, give and even teach. But the Spirit wants to ask you the question Paul asked Corinth: how do you respond when someone else is honoured? When another person's ministry grows faster than yours, when another believer is praised in front of you, when your opinion is passed over for someone else's — what happens inside you? Jealousy and strife are the marks of a baby, not a giant. The Spirit is not condemning you. He is telling you that you are meant to grow, and that the way to solid food runs straight through the death of your need to be first.

items.title: What Are You Building With?
items.body: Everyone builds. The question is the material. Look honestly at your work — your ministry, your career, your family, your service. How much of it is gold, silver and costly stones: slow, costly obedience, done with love and pure motives, according to the truth? And how much is wood, hay and stubble: fast, cheap, impressive for a moment, done for applause or numbers or self-protection? The fire is coming, and it will not ask how big your work was, how many people saw it or how much they praised it. It will ask what it was made of. The Spirit is asking you to change the materials now, while there is still time to build.

items.title: You Are Standing in the Holy of Holies
items.body: There is a church you are frustrated with. There are believers you find difficult, a leader you resent, a group you complain about. The Spirit wants you to see them the way Paul saw Corinth: “Don’t you know that you are a temple of God, and that God’s Spirit lives in you?” The flawed, irritating people you worship with are the dwelling place of the Most High God. The words you say about them, the divisions you encourage, the gossip you pass on — those are not neutral. They are either building up the sanctuary or tearing it down. Ask the Spirit to show you whether your words this month have been building God's temple or vandalising it.

audit.title: The Maturity Check
audit.body: Name one person in your church, ministry, workplace or family whose success makes you uncomfortable. Write down honestly what you feel when they are praised. If the answer is jealousy, resentment or a desire to see them taken down a notch, that is the clearest evidence of verse 3 in your life. Confess it specifically, by name, to God.

audit.title: The Materials Check
audit.body: List the three main things you are investing your time and energy in right now. Beside each one, write one honest sentence about your motive: why are you really doing it? Then ask: if the fire of verse 13 tested this today, would it be gold, silver and costly stones, or wood, hay and stubble? Do not answer quickly. Motives are part of the material.

audit.title: The Ownership Check
audit.body: Verse 21 says “let no one boast in men.” Is there a human leader, teacher or movement whose approval you need more than Christ's? Would you feel lost if they rejected you? Write down the name. Then read verses 21 to 23 aloud and remind yourself: that person belongs to you as a gift from God; you belong to Christ.

practices.title: Honouring a Rival
practices.body: This week, do the opposite of jealousy. Choose the person whose success you named in the Maturity Check. Find a genuine reason to thank God for them, and then tell them — or tell someone else, in their hearing or in writing — specifically what God is doing through them. Do it without qualification and without mentioning yourself. Then pray for their work to grow even more. You will feel the milk bottle being taken away. That is the point.

practices.title: Rebuilding With Gold
practices.body: Pick one area of your life or ministry where you know you have been building with straw — cutting corners, doing it for show, chasing numbers, or working without love. Write down one concrete change that would turn it into gold: a hidden act of service no one will see, a slower and more faithful approach, a conversation you have avoided, a motive you need to surrender. Do that one thing before the week ends. Then write verse 14 on a card — “If any man’s work remains which he built on it, he will receive a reward” — and keep it where you work.

prayerReflection: “Father, I confess that I have been a baby with a beard. I have known much and grown little. I have been jealous when others were honoured, and I have stirred up strife and taken sides. Forgive me for walking in the ways of men. Take away the milk and grow me up into the meat of Your Word. Lord, I thank You that I am Your field and Your building, and that You let me work beside You. Whatever I have planted or watered, You gave the growth — and You are giving it still, underground, where I cannot see. Keep me from stealing the credit, and keep me from despairing when I cannot see the harvest. You pay for faithful labour, not for visible success. Jesus, You are the only foundation. I am standing on You. Now show me what I am building with. Burn away the wood, hay and stubble in my life now, while there is still time to rebuild. Give me the patience to build with gold, silver and costly stones, slowly, faithfully, in love. When the Day comes, let my work remain. Holy Spirit, You live in Your church. Forgive me for every word I have spoken that tore down Your temple. Teach me to see the people I worship with as Your dwelling place. And Father, thank You that all things are mine — life, death, the present, the future — because I am Christ's, and Christ is Yours. I need no other master. In Jesus' name, Amen.”

storyConnections.title: Bezalel, the Spirit-Filled Master Builder
storyConnections.summary: When God gave Moses the plans for the tabernacle — the first dwelling place of His presence among Israel — He did not leave the building to whoever was available. He called Bezalel by name and filled him with the Spirit of God, in wisdom, understanding and knowledge, to work in gold, silver and bronze and in cutting stones. Bezalel and Oholiab built exactly according to the pattern God gave, and the people brought so much material that Moses had to tell them to stop giving. When the work was finished, the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle. Paul calls himself a “wise master builder” in verse 10, building God's dwelling place in Corinth. The pattern is the same: the Spirit's wisdom, the right materials, faithfulness to God's design, and a building God can fill with His glory.

storyConnections.title: The Tower That Was Built for a Name
storyConnections.summary: On the plain of Shinar, humanity gathered to build a city and a tower reaching to the heavens, using bricks baked hard in fire and tar for mortar. Their stated purpose was candid: let us make a name for ourselves. It was impressive, it was unified, and it was built entirely on human wisdom and for human glory. God came down, confused their language, and scattered them, and the building stopped. Babel is the opposite of 1 Corinthians 3. It shows what happens when people build to make a name for themselves rather than on the foundation God has laid. Corinth's factions were a small Babel: each group building its own reputation around its own preferred leader. God's answer to both is the same — He alone gives the increase, and no flesh will boast before Him.

storyConnections.title: Shouting and Weeping Over a Foundation
storyConnections.summary: When the exiles returned from Babylon to a ruined Jerusalem, one of the first things they did was lay the foundation of a new temple. The priests blew trumpets, the Levites clashed cymbals, and the people sang that the LORD is good and His lovingkindness endures forever. But many of the older priests and leaders, who had seen the glory of Solomon's temple, wept aloud at the sight of this smaller foundation, while others shouted for joy, so that no one could tell the sound of joy from the sound of weeping. A foundation is easy to underestimate because you cannot see what will be built on it yet. Paul says the only foundation that matters has already been laid — Jesus Christ — and what is built on it will be revealed in time. Do not despise the day of small foundations. What matters is what is built on them, and with what.
